text: Managing outbreaks of the citrus long-horned beetle Anoplophora chinensis (Forster) in Europe: molecular diagnosis of plant infestation

BACKGROUND: Anoplophora chinensis (Forster) (Coleoptera Cerambycidae) is a polyphagous long-horned beetle native toEastern Asia that infests a wide range of broadleaved plants, causing disruption of vascular tissue, structural weakness and tree death. As a result, A. chinensis is a quarantine pest for the European Union. In order to confirm its infestations on plants, it is necessary to obtain adult or larval specimens on which morphological or molecular analysis can be performed. However, obtaining such specimens from infested plants can be a demanding and difficult task. Therefore, a diagnostic tool that is non-invasive for the plant and able to be performed in the absence of any insect stages may be useful to confirm infestations of A. chinensis on plants.RESULTS: A protocol is presented that is based on polymerase chain reaction amplification using DNA extracted from A. chinensis faecal material collected in the field. CONCLUSION: Results obtained in the present work show that the non-invasive approach is a reliable and accurate alternative diagnostic tool in phytosanitary surveys.

Anoplophora chinensis (Forster) (Coleoptera Cerambycidae) is a polyphagous long-horned beetle native to Eastern Asia (China, Japan, Korea). It is commonly known as the citrus long-horned beetle (CLB) owing to the severe damage it causes in citrus orchards in Eastern Asia. 1 -4 A. chinensis can attack a wide range of broadleaved plants, including potted plants, 'bonsais' and old and monumental types of forest, urban, fruit and ornamental trees and shrubs. 3 -6 A. chinensis generally colonises healthy trees, but can repeatedly attack the same trees over a long period of time. The larvae disrupt the vascular tissue of the plant, causing structural weakness and tree death. 4 A. chinensis requires 1-3 years for juvenile development, depending on the prevailing climatic conditions, among other factors. After mating, females lay their eggs mainly at the trunk base of susceptible plants during the growing season. Larvae are initially phloem feeders; they then develop into xylem feeders, digging galleries in the wood. Adult beetles finally emerge from infested trees by chewing the thin portion of wood and bark separating the pupal chamber from the external environment, 3,4 resulting in a circular exit hole (1-2 cm in diameter).
A. chinensis is an extremely damaging pest that is specified on the quarantine lists of Europe, the United States and Canada. 7 It is subjected to strong European phytosanitary regulations to prevent its introduction and spread. Eradication measures have been put in place to curb the spread of infestations. 8 Outbreaks of A. chinensis have been reported in northern Italy near Milan (first observed in 2001) and in Rome, central Italy (first observed in 2008). 8 Other European nations have also reported infestations. 4,6,8,9 The eradication measures for A. chinensis stipulate the destruction of infested trees and severe regulations and restrictions on global and local trade and the establishment of host plants. 4,6,9,10 These eradication measures have adverse financial effects on plant growers, sellers and individuals in related commercial activities.
The mandatory monitoring activities involve inspecting plants for the presence of adult exit holes and/or larval frass at the base. This allows positive diagnosis of infestation even during periods when the adult beetle itself is not observed on the plant. However, the presence of exit holes and larval frass are non-specific indicators of the presence and activity of xylophagous insects inside the trunk of the plants. There are several European xylophagous insects that have similar signs of activity to those produced by A. chinensis.
These European insects include different species of Coleoptera (included in the genera Morimus, Saperda, Herophila, Aromia, etc.) and of Lepidoptera (included in the families Cossidae, Sesidae, etc.). In addition, other non-native species present in Europe, such as Anoplophora glabripennis (Motschulsky) and Psacothea hilaris (Pascoe), 8 also show similar signs of activity when infesting plants. Confirming the presence of A. chinensis in plants infested by xylophagous insects is difficult, and yet it is fundamental for the success of prevention/eradication strategies against the pest. The possibility of using non-invasive molecular techniques to analyse larval frass from xylophagous insects is therefore an attractive procedure for diagnosing A. chinensis infestation during phytosanitary surveys.
The use of DNA extracted from faecal material is a welldeveloped approach in non-destructive molecular analysis, especially in mammals and birds. 11 -13 However, there is limited literature on the application of molecular analysis using DNA extracted from faecal samples in insects. 14 -16 In the present study, the possibility of developing a diagnostic test to confirm the presence of A. chinensis from environmental frass samples was investigated. Frass samples consist of plant material mixed with insect faeces, and it potentially retains traces of the insect's DNA.
The purpose of this work was to develop a molecular diagnostic tool based on polymerase chain reaction that amplifies faecal DNA using a primer pair specific for A. chinensis.

A. chinensis adults were obtained directly from infested host plants in Rome (Italy). Adults of Morimus asper (Sulzer), Aromia moscata (Linnaeus), Herophila tristis (Linnaeus) and Monochamus galloprovincialis (Olivier) and larvae of Zeuzera pyrina (Linnaeus) and Paranthrene tabaniformis (Rottemburg) were collected during field entomological surveys in central Italy. Adult specimens of A. glabripennis were obtained from infested host plants in Cornuda (Italy), while larvae of P. hilaris were obtained from laboratoryreared colonies originating from host plants naturally infested in northern Italy. Collected insects were stored in 95% ethanol until molecular analysis.

Insect legs or the last segments of larvae were dissected in a clockglass cup. DNA was extracted using a modified CTAB-PVP protocol 17 in which 100 µg of proteinase K (Roche, Indianapolis, IN) was added to the extraction buffer. The pellet was resuspended in 500 µL of TE and extracted using the phenol-chloroform protocol, followed by alcoholic precipitation. DNA was resuspended in ddH 2 O and evaluated with both a Smart Spec Plus spectrophotometer (Bio-Rad) and agarose gel.

Specific 24-mer primers (Chinensis) were designed on the basis of sequences derived from A. chinensis, A. glabripennis, H. tristis, M. asper, A. moschata, M. galloprovincialis, P. hilaris, Z. pyrina and P. tabaniformis specimens and from DNA sequences present in the nucleotide database of NCBI [Saperda carcharias (Linnaeus) and Leiopus nebulosus (Linnaeus)]. Sequences of the primer pair for Chinensis are as follows: ChinensisF: 5 -CATAAGATTTTGATTACTTCCACC-3 , and ChinensisR: 5 -TTTCGA TCTGTAAGAAGTATTGTG-3 . The predicted amplification product was 345 bp long.
Another primer, called 1859F, was designed, starting from C1-J-1859, 18 and subsequently adapted on the basis of A. chinensis, A. glabripennis, M. asper, H. tristis, A. moschata, M. galloprovincialis and Z. piryna sequences. The primers 1859F and HCO2198 19 are known to be able to amplify a fragment of the 5 region of the mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase subunit I (COI) gene, which is 365 bp long. 18 The sequence of primer 1859F is 5 -GGAACNGGNTGAACWGTTTAYCCNCC-3 . Degenerate bases were included to ensure amplification in a wider number of arthropods.
Features and localisation of the primers are summarised in Fig. 1 and Table 1.
The primers were synthesised at Eurofins MWG Operon, Ebersberg, Germany.

All PCR amplification mixtures (50 µL) contained 50 mM of KCl, 10 mM of Tris HCl (pH 8.8), 0.01% Tween 20, 1.5 mM of MgCl 2 , 0.4 mM of dNTP, 6.0 µM of each primer and 2.5 units of Taq DNA polymerase (AppliChem, Darmstadt, Germany).
The PCR thermal programme for amplification using primer pair HCO2198-LCO1490 19 consisted of an initial denaturation step for 2 min at 94 • C, followed by 45 cycles of 1 min at 94 • C, 1.5 min at 45 • C and 1.5 min at 72 • C, and then a final elongation step for 7 min at 72 • C.
The 1859F-HCO2198 PCR thermal programme consisted of initial denaturation for 2 min at 94 • C, followed by 45 cycles of 1 min at 94 • C, 1 min at 50 • C and 1 min at 72 • C, with a final extension of 5 min at 72 • C.
The Chinensis PCR thermal programme consisted of an initial denaturation step for 2 min at 94 • C, followed by 45 cycles of 1 min at 94 • C, 1.5 min at 60 • C and 1 min at 72 • C, and then final elongation for 7 min at 72 • C.

PCR suitability of genomic DNA was assessed using PCR with the primers HCO2198-LCO1490 and 150 ng of DNA as template. The specificity of Chinensis primers was tested using the same quantity of DNA as in Chinensis PCR.

section: collection of frass produced by various xylophagous insects
text: Larval frass of A. chinensis was collected from host plants in the two infested sites (Lombardy and Rome) in Italy. Samples were collected in Lombardy during phytosanitary surveys from naturally infested plants, during which A. chinensis larvae were extracted from plant stems to confirm the identity of the insect. In Rome, frass was collected from infested wooden material and kept in insect cages until adult A. chinensis emerged. These collection procedures ensured that the frass collected at both sites belonged to A. chinensis. Samples were collected in June-July 2011 (Rome) and in November 2011 (Lombardy). Frass was collected in 50 mL plastic vials from host plants, using clean spoons. Within 6 h of collection from the field, samples were stored at -20  Table 1. Primer sequences and their melting temperature. For each primer pair were reported amplicon length and annealing temperature used collected in total. Larval frass of other xylophagous insects (M. asper, A. moscata, H. tristis, M. galloprovincialis and Z. pyrina) were obtained from infested plant hosts collected in the field or from artificially infested plants. During the collection of larval frass, it was not possible to assess the amount of time that had elapsed since its production.

Frass was gently shaken inside collecting vials, and top layers, enriched with wood chippings, were discarded. About 100 mg of fine-grain frass was collected for each sample. DNA was extracted with the ZymoResearch Faecal DNA MicroPrep kit (Zymo Research Corporation, Irvine, CA) according to the manufacturer's protocol upon the addition of 0.5% β-mercaptoethanol to the DNA-binding buffer. DNA was eluted in a volume of 30 µL of elution buffer provided with the DNA extraction kit.

A quantity of 5 µL of frass-extracted DNA was used in HCO2198-LCO1490 PCR. DNA fragments were purified using the Nucleo Spin Extract II kit (Macherey-Nagel, Hoerd, France) and analysed by agarose gel electrophoresis. The presence of amplicons derived from insect DNA was verified with 1859F-HCO2198 PCR, with 5 µL of the purified HCO2198-LCO1490 amplicon as a template. The detection of A. chinensis DNA was performed using the same volume of purified fragments as in Chinensis PCR. A positive control reaction with 150 ng of A. chinensis genomic DNA was included in all PCR using a Chinensis primer pair.

section: accuracy and repeatability of the diagnostic protocol
text: Accuracy was evaluated using frass DNA extracted from ten different plants that were clearly infested with A. chinensis according to the diagnostic protocol previously described. Repeatability was evaluated using two different frass samples positive for Chinensis. Each sample was divided into three aliquots of 100 mg each of fine-powdered frass; six independent DNA extractions were performed on each of the aliquots. All samples were tested according to previously described diagnostic protocols. Carlsbad, CA) and agarose gel electrophoresis. The detection limit of the diagnostic protocol was assessed using serial dilutions of the HCO2198-LCO1490 PCR fragment as a template for Chinensis PCR.

DNA shelf life was evaluated using larval frass samples collected inside insect galleries of artificially infested plants (A. negundo, A. hippocastanum and C. × sinensis). Plants were artificially infested by placing a single host plant and three pairs of adults in the same insect cage. Females laid their eggs at the base of the plant, and larval presence was assessed by observing the production of frass expelled from the plant and accumulated at its base.
After removal of the adult insects from the cages, infested plants were stored inside a multicompartmentalised walk-in insect cage for 1, 2 and 3 years under ambient climatic conditions (artificial infestations of plants were performed respectively in 2009, 2010 and 2011). A. chinensis adult specimens successfully emerged from the infested plants 1 year after the artificial infestation. At the time of testing (2012), larval frass was collected inside the insect galleries in the artificially infested plants after removal of the bark tissue. About 150 mg of fine-grain frass was collected for each sample. DNA was extracted and analysed with protocols previously described.
2.12 DNA sequencing PCR products were sequenced at the Centro di Servizi per le Biotecnologie di Interesse Agrario Chimico ed Industriale (CIBIACI), Università degli Studi di Firenze, Italy.

In order to obtain a diagnostic PCR for A. chinensis identification, the full barcode region of mitochondrial gene COI was amplified and sequenced for nine xylophagous insect species belonging to two different insect orders, Lepidoptera and Coleoptera. DNA extractions were tested for the presence of PCR inhibitors using the HCO2198-LCO1490 primer pair, and all samples were successfully amplified (Fig. 2A). Chinensis primers showed the ability selectively to amplify the A. chinensis COI fragment in the PCR conditions reported in Section 2 (Fig. 2B).

section: evaluation of dna extracted from frass
text: DNA samples from different trees infested by A. chinensis showed variable shapes, from the high-molecular-weight single band (Fig. 3A, lanes 4, 5, 7, 8, 9 and 11) to the smeared DNA (Fig. 3A, lanes 3 and 10). All samples could be amplified with the HCO2198-LCO1490 primer pair (Fig. 3B), including samples 1 and 5, the frass-extracted DNA of which was too little to be detected on agarose gel.

The diagnostic protocol was tested using the frass of some xylophagous insects that may be mistaken for A. chinensis. Frass-extracted DNA samples can be amplified using the HCO2198-LCO1490 primer pair (Fig. 4A), confirming the absence of PCR inhibitors in DNA extractions. PCR with the 1859F-HCO2198 primer pair enabled the conclusion to be drawn that all samples tested positive for the presence of insect DNA (Fig. 4B). Positive results with the Chinensis primers were only reported in A. chinensis samples and not in other cerambycids or lepidopterans tested (Fig. 4C). Positive results with 1859F-HCO2198 and Chinensis primers were further confirmed by sequencing.

section: accuracy and repeatability of the diagnostic protocol
text:
The diagnostic protocol was performed on ten independent frass samples (Fig. 3) obtained from ten A. chinensis-infested trees, which gave eight positive amplifications and two negative results (samples 1 and 5) (Fig. 5A). Positive results were confirmed by sequencing.
The repeatability of the diagnostic protocol was tested on two A. chinensis-positive samples, with three independent DNA extractions being performed on each sample. All six samples analysed using the previously reported diagnostic protocol gave positive results (Fig. 5B). Data suggest homogeneity in faecal DNA content inside fine-grain frass.

section: detection limit of the diagnostic protocol
text: In the absence of other DNA except for the A. chinensis HCO2198-LCO1490 fragment, clear amplification was observed with 4 ng of template (Fig. 6). It is assumed that this value is the lower amount of A. chinensis DNA that can be detected.

DNA shelf life was evaluated using frass samples collected from galleries of artificially infested trunks. The diagnostic protocol was able to give positive results in frass samples obtained from trunks where the infestation was 1, 2 and 3 years old (Fig. 7).

Currently, the diagnosis of A. chinensis infestation on plants can only be confirmed by obtaining adult specimens of the beetle or performing molecular analysis on juveniles, which must be extracted from the wooden tissues of the plant. Moreover, obtaining specimens of A. chinensis from infested plants can sometimes be impossible because in some cases the adults may leave the plant before the phytosanitary inspection occurs. Moreover in many cases, infestations of A. chinensis occur in cities on large, old, ornamental and monumental trees growing along streets and in parks, which are normally designated as protected trees owing to their historical conservation status.
A non-invasive diagnostic approach for suspected A. chinensis infestation will prevent unnecessary plant injuries or plant destruction that may negatively affect urban plant structure and will also help preserve human and economic resources.
Extensive literature is available on mammalian and bird identification from dung samples, while molecular scatology is an established procedure in diet analysis of wildlife terrestrial and aquatic organisms. 20,21 Mammalian dung has different characteristics to insect faeces. Insects are uricotelic organisms; therefore, their dejections contain variable amounts of uric acid and allantoin, which both have chemical properties that allow considerable reduction of water loss to the larva. Insect dejections are typically dehydrated, reducing the enzymatic activity of digestive DNAses on expulsion and thus enhancing the DNA stability in frass samples compared with mammalian dung.
In spite of many researchers hypothesising the use of insect faeces as a non-destructive source of DNA, hitherto the studies done have focused mainly on faecal samples collected from laboratory-reared insect colonies. However, it is important to investigate the possibility of extracting PCR-quality DNA from field insect frass, as frass from laboratory colonies is relatively less exposed to environmental conditions than field frass. Furthermore, in intensive rearing conditions, where many specimens share the same cage, a greater number of epithelial cells desquamate and accumulate, resulting in a higher amount of DNA per milligram of frass than in a field frass sample.
Considering that faeces have a substantially lower number of epithelial cells, it was decided to focus on PCR primers on a target located on mtDNA, the quantity of which relative to nuclear DNA increases the chances of recovering sufficient PCR-quality DNA. Furthermore, the analysis of 40 Italian A. chinensis samples showed no polymorphisms in the COI gene, making the gene an ideal target for the present diagnostic protocol. In addition, COI is a well-known gene commonly used as a standard in species identification.
The main problem in DNA extraction from xylophagous insect frass is the high amount of PCR inhibitors within samples; hence, a DNA extraction kit specific for faeces was used. Although the chemical properties of the inhibitors were not investigated,  a brown genomic DNA pellet was observed after alcoholic precipitation, suggesting the presence of quinone and polyphenol molecules (Strangi A et al., unpublished data). A preliminary amplification using the generic primer HCO2198-LCO1490 was performed to assess the suitability of frass-extracted DNA for PCR reactions. This primer pair can amplify a larger region of the COI gene containing the Chinensis fragment. This PCR is an essential positive control to ensure an inhibitor-free DNA preparation. As the DNA extraction protocol was successfully conducted on frass from various plant species, it can be concluded that the same protocol can be successfully applied to a wide range of plants attacked by xylophagous insects.
Sequencing of HCO2198-LCO1490 amplification products resulted in multiple overlapping signals from the sample. This was probably due to a mixture of barcode fragments belonging to various organisms present in the samples. The presence of DNA from various organisms in the samples appears to be a plausible explanation, because direct amplification with Chinensis primer on frass-extracted DNA gave rise to multiple and variable bands in addition to the specific ones (data not shown). Unambiguous results were obtained when a nested PCR was performed on the HCO2198-LCO1490 fragment using Chinensis primers. The primers could retain their specificity in the presence of A. chinensis and non-A. chinensis amplicons generated with HCO2198-LCO1490 Diagnostic PCR performed on HCO2198-LCO1490 fragments of frass (Figs 3B and 5A) obtained from different A. chinensis-infested trees resulted in eight of the ten samples testing positive for A. chinensis. Samples in lanes 6 and 8 (Figs 3B and5A) confirm the hypothesis that the HCO2198-LCO1490 amplification is a mixture of barcode fragments with variable contributions from A. chinensis mtDNA. Samples 1 and 5 (Fig. 5A) have no evident amplification products in lane 5, and show two non-specific bands in lane 1. It can be hypothesised that, in those samples where frass-extracted DNA is not visible on agarose gel (Fig. 3A), A. chinensis DNA was degraded by environmental agents. Following this hypothesis, it can be assumed that the HCO2198-LCO1490 fragments originated from DNA belonging to organisms that were incidentally collected with frass (e.g. mites), which explains the multiple overlapping signals in the chromatograms.
The precision of diagnostic procedures is linked to the stability of insect frass DNA. The detection limit of this diagnostic protocol was found to be 4 ng of the HCO2198-LCO1490 A. chinensis-specific fragment. It was observed that HCO2198-LCO1490 amplification products from frass-extracted DNA contain this quantity in a volume of 5 µL. The minimum concentration of frass-extracted DNA was not used as a reference because samples contain variable amounts of target and non-target DNA. However, it was observed that significant amplification of HCO2198-LCO1490 A. chinensis fragments occurs when a minimum of 0.015 ng of genomic  DNA is extracted from adults or larvae (data not shown). This finding cannot be extended to the diagnostic procedure under investigation in this study because it does not represent the competitive PCR conditions that prevail when frass-extracted DNA is used as a template. Within the detection limit, the diagnostic protocol gave highly repeatable results for all samples analysed. This confirms that the main source of variability is DNA stability within faecal material.
The diagnostic protocol using DNA extracted from frass collected inside the trunks was able to detect A. chinensis even 3 years after infestation, showing a long intrinsic shelf life of faecal DNA belonging to the xylophagous insect.
Frass can also persist externally on the ground near the trunk bases for variable times, depending on the environmental conditions. In isolated urban trees, collectors can find frass up to a maximum of 10 days after its expulsion from the gallery; after this period, frass is commonly dispersed by atmospheric agents and human activities. The timeline can be prolonged up to 3 months in natural park trees, especially where the trunk bases are surrounded by grass.
In spite of a long shelf life, exposed faecal DNA can easily undergo degradation during a short period in the field. As demonstrated in other work, 22 many biotic and abiotic factors can significantly affect the kinetic parameters of extracellular DNA degradation. For this reason, particular attention must be paid to the sampling procedure: collectors must be able to distinguish frass exposed for long times in ambient conditions from newly expelled frass, and use only fresh samples because there is a greater chance of recovering faecal DNA suitable for PCR. This approach could reduce the systematic error in the sampling protocol introduced by environmental degradation of faecal DNA, thereby increasing the precision of the diagnostic technique.
Results obtained in the present study show that it is possible accurately and reliably to diagnose A. chinensis infestation through the analysis of larval frass collected in the field. This approach offers a new diagnostic tool in phytosanitary surveys and can be used to inspect plants for A.chinensis infestation at entry ports, during plant trading and as a plant management tool for urban municipalities.
